The [starter](../../starters/threadx-riscv64.md) scaffolded a talker for
`board = "rv-virt-threadx"`, Eclipse ThreadX with its NetX Duo TCP/IP stack
on QEMU's RISC-V 64 `virt` machine, and heard it from ROS 2. This page covers
what comes after it: the image's network configuration, what is particular to
this board and its architecture port, and the native build. Sched tasks are
declared the same way on both ThreadX boards; the
[ThreadX Linux simulator](threadx-linux.md#run-sched-tasks) page shows them.

## Configure the platform

The guest boots behind QEMU's user-mode network, so its image states the
router's address as the guest sees it and names a board network file for its
own address:

```toml
[image.threadx]
board = "rv-virt-threadx"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:9400"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]
```

and `board-net.toml`, beside `system.toml` in the bringup:

```toml
[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 15
```

`10.0.2.2` is QEMU's gateway, which forwards to the host, so a router
listening on the host's `0.0.0.0` at the `locator`'s port is reachable. An
image that states no address gets QEMU's first guest address, `10.0.2.15`;
`host = N` picks `10.0.2.N`. With no `locator`, as scaffolded, the image
dials `tcp/10.0.2.2:7447`. Start the router as the starter did, with its
`listen/endpoints` port changed to the one the image dials (`9400` here).

The node package does not change between this board and the
[Linux simulator](threadx-linux.md): only the image's `board` line and its
network keys do, and one bringup can hold an image for each.

## Board notes

- **QEMU's `virt` machine, a 64-bit RISC-V core.** The UART is on standard
  input and output, and the network is a virtio-net device on QEMU's
  user-mode network. `nros setup rv-virt-threadx` fetches the RISC-V 64
  cross-compiler and `qemu-system-riscv64`.
- **Three ThreadX packages in three layers.** `nros-board-threadx` is the
  family driver (the kernel and NetX Duo build, and the boot path both boards
  call). `nros-board-threadx-port-riscv64` is the architecture port.
  `nros-board-threadx-qemu-riscv64` is the board overlay: defaults, console,
  exit, panic and network bring-up. The generated entry depends on the board
  crate, so nothing you write names any of them.
- **Why the architecture port exists.** Upstream's RISC-V 64 port types
  `ULONG` as 8 bytes, and NetX Duo's packet code assumes 4. nano-ros retypes
  it to `unsigned int`, as upstream's own Linux and AArch64 ports do, and
  that shifts the offsets the port's context-switch assembly loads, so the
  assembly is forked with it. A second RISC-V 64 ThreadX board reuses the
  port unchanged and writes only an overlay; see
  [Add a board](../../extending/add-a-board.md).
- **Search the port's `inc/` first** if you build ThreadX outside
  `nros build`, before `$THREADX_DIR/ports/risc-v64/gnu/inc`. In the wrong
  order the build succeeds against the 8-byte `ULONG` and packets corrupt at
  run time. A `_Static_assert(sizeof(ULONG) == 4, …)` in the board's hooks
  turns the mistake into a build failure.
- **No physical ThreadX board ships.** A vendor board (Renesas Synergy,
  i.MX RT and others) is a board package of your own on the family crate,
  flashed with that vendor's tools; see [Flash a real board](flash-a-real-board.md).

## Read the run plan

From the starter's workspace, print the plan `nros run` follows:

```bash probe=410
nros run tx_node --dry-run --why
```

The plan names the QEMU runner and the `qemu:rv-virt` machine, the console on
the guest's UART, and the link to the router at the image's `locator`.
`--why` names where each fact came from, the board's descriptor for most of
them.

## Drive the native build yourself

The first build compiles ThreadX and NetX Duo, about three minutes; later
builds take seconds. Print the exact cargo or CMake commands, and the QEMU
line the run uses, without building:

```bash probe=420
nros build --dry-run
```

`nros configure` writes the generated entry without building. Neither
command's output under `build/` is yours to edit.

## If it doesn't work

- **The image boots and never publishes:** no router on the host's
  `0.0.0.0` at the `locator`'s port. A router on `127.0.0.1` is unreachable
  from the guest.
- **Corrupted packets in a ThreadX build of your own:** the include order
  above.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshoot](../deploy/troubleshoot.md).
